description.narrative: Reporting is an important management tool which is used to inform relevant government officials and other stakeholders about the results being achieved by individual projects and the programme as a whole. For project partners, it is compulsory to use the prescribed Orange Knowledge annual report format in order to report on project achievements. The annual report also provides valuable data on the financial situation of the project. Based on an analysis of the project performance in relation to the project output(s) and expected outcome(s), a revision of the project work plan may be suggested by the project partners. The consequences of a possible revision on the project work plan and budget must be made clear in the annual report. Nuffic monitors outputs and outcomes and not activities . Therefore, the main focus of the annual report must be on the achievement of the project’s output(s) and planned outcome(s). The information provided in the annual reports of the projects is used by Nuffic to monitor the progress of the project and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other stakeholders about the output(s) and outcome(s) being achieved by individual projects and the Orange Knowledge programme as a whole. Please note that if project progress is in accordance with the original planning, reporting requirements are minimal. Only in case of deviations from the planning, more elaboration is demanded. In the grant award letter, the dates for submission of the annual reports are mentioned. In case of a three-year project, between 5-7 reports are obligatory. The first report (0) is a very short report which focuses on specific conditions and/or recommendations in the grant. There is no need to report on progress in achieving outputs and outcomes, which is done in the first annual report. As annex to the report 0, the consortium agreements between the partners should be submitted. The final report must reflect on the entire project period.

actual.value:
Although the original project dates were from 1 December 2019 to 30 October 2020, due to the COVID-19 pandemic, two no-cost extensions were requested and thus project end was on the 31 October 2021. The two remaining activities under this project for 2021 was the development of a Nutrion sensitive training curriculum and the development of two case study videos.
- The curriculum developed is nutrition-sensitive agriculture module offered as an inter-colleges module for both the agriculture and health colleges students and will highlight the importance of both sectors contribution to the food and nutrition security of farm households in the Yamfo area and Ghana at large. Please see the curriculum attached.
- The internship for the video’s. At the end of 2020 Terms of Reference for the internship for internship were drafted students recruited for the assignment. Initially we planned to have 2 students from the Wageningen University & Research and 2 Ghanaian students. This did not worked out (see for more details section 3, bottlenecks) and thus we adjusted the assignment to work with 4 Ghanaian students (2 from the College of Health – Yamfo and 2 from the Kwadaso Agric College). Although ideally also among the students we would like to have a gender balance but that was unfortunately not feasible and we had 3 male and 1 female student. We had two cases studies in mind, but because the project only managed to work with the Ghanaian students and for 2 months instead of planned 4 months, the project only worked on 1 case study. The project “Planting for food and jobs” by the Ghana Government as an example for communities based nutrition sensitive agricultural project.
- The selected case study should reflect on (i) if and how the programme contributes to food and nutrition security of the farming households and community members reached (ii) to what extend the programme follows a nutrition-sensitive approach and (iii) if and how human rights principles are considered in programme design and implementation. In the end despite all the efforts and we manage to have instead of a full case study and set of 8 videos explaining 8 of the 10 recommendations of nutrition-sensitive agriculture.

The grant was issued in late 2019 and the started on the 1 of December 2018. The activities that took place during 2019 were:
- Inform the counterpart that we did win TMT training - Start the process of drafting a co-operation agreement between WCDI and College of Health Yamfo - Together with the counter part planned the activities for 2020 - Make a detailed budget and go through the financial procedure with the counterpart

The planning for the three trainings for 2020 starting in May 2020 came to halt when the COVID pandemic hit in March 2020 countries went in lock-down and the facilitators were informed by their University that they were not allowed to be travelling. The following activities took place in 2020 but later then planned.
- Revision of the work plan and training approach from face-2-face to a hybrid trainings where the participants in Ghana would come together in a COVID-19 proof meeting room (larger then initially planned to make sure the mandatory distance can be observed) and the facilitators will call in from the Netherlands via Zoom.
- Revision of the budget, as travel and lodging costs for the facilitators could not be spend due to the world-wide lock down. In addition, to observe the COVID-19 measures meeting, local travel cost increased as larger venue and larger busses needed to be hired. In addition, extra intern bandwidth needed to be obtained to ensure optimal connections for the facilitators from the Netherlands. These were al inline with the NUFFIC adjustments that were allowed due to COVID-19 pandemic.
- In August 2020, the first training of 20 teachers from 3 institutions, namely College of Health – Yamfo, Kwadaso Agric College and Ejura Agric College were trained in Rights-based approach to linking Agriculture and Food and Nutrition Security. This 5-days training took the participants through the concepts of Food and Nutrition Security, the linkages between agriculture and food and nutrition security also looking form a rights-based approach perspectives, the pathways from agriculture to nutrition and discussed also the important of stakeholder partnerships. Please see detailed training programme attached.
- In September 2020, 20 participants from the Ghana health Services, Department of Agriculture and other organizations were trained. The latter Participants came from CHAG, HortiFresh, Holystic Nutrition Organisation, Human Care and Maintenance Foundation and Yedent Agro Group of Companies. 5-day training with the tittle Rights-based approach to linking Agriculture and Food and Nutrition Security took the participants through the concepts of Food and Nutrition Security, the linkages between agriculture and food and nutrition security also looking form a rights-based approach perspective and discussed also the important of stakeholder partnerships. Please see detailed training programme attached.
- The last training in October 2020 was for 20 policy makers from the Ghana health Services, the Department of Agriculture, the Netherlands Embassy, the College of Health – Yamfo. This 2-day training: 2-day multi-stakeholder engagement workshop to improved household food and nutrition security in the Ahafo Region focused not only on the understanding of Food and Nutrition Security link with agriculture, but also on the importance of nutrition governance. At the end of the two days with regional and district nutrition coordination committees and workplan for the next steps.
- After these training two major activities remained, namely the video case study and the development of a Nutrion sensitive training curriculum. The planning for both activities were made and a TOR for the making of the video as students were to be recruited to make the movie.
